newsitem.title: GREECE: GNN FEATURE:SIMITIS STRUGGLING IN NATIONAL ELECTION CAMPAIGN.
newsitem.headline: GNN FEATURE:SIMITIS STRUGGLING IN NATIONAL ELECTION CAMPAIGN.

text.p: Greece's socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis called early elections this month confident of an easy win but he has failed to inspire voters and is fighting for his political life.

Instead of an easy romp to his first elected term, Simitis has come up against a wall of voter indifference and fears among many leftists that he is little more than a neo-conservative who will impose stringent economic measures.
Opinion polls ahead of Sunday's election have shown Simitis, 60, running neck and neck with the new conservative party leader Miltiades Evert, 57.

Most embarrassing for both men is that droves of voters have turned their backs on the two parties which have dominated Greek politics for 20 years, saying they will vote for one of the many smaller groups in the race.

Little parties, rarely an important force in Greek politics, could prove to be giant killers this time. The smaller leftist parties have been bleeding off crucial socialist votes and that has Simitis running scared.
Opinion polls show four peripheral parties -- three on the left, one on the right -- taking a total of 18 to 20 percent of the national vote.
Major parties -- Simitis's Panhellenic Socialist Movement (PASOK) and Evert's New Democracy -- have a combined vote of only 60 percent.
"Neither major party has been able to win the support of a third of the Greek electorate. It's something we have not seen before," said television poll analyst Elias Nikolakopoulos.
That dismal showing is attributed to massive voter apathy, a a lack of real differences on economic and foreign policy and an absence of any charismatic political figure in the race.
"Their policy differences are more in style than substance," Thanos Veremis, the head of the Hellenic Foundation for European and Foreign Policy, said.
Both men will have to dance to the European Union's tune on the economy. Pressure from the EU, the United States and others will prevent dangerous adventures with Turkey or in the Balkans.
"In foreign policy we see no difference in their content, just their style. In economics we see some differences but both are constrained really by EU targets," said one EU diplomat.
In style Simitis appears cool, almost passive, and is most at ease in discussing the details of foreign or economic plans -- which leaves voters more drowsy than inspired.

The media calls him "the Chinese" for his demure manner, slight build, almond eyes and inscrutable expression. From the outset he said he would campaign quietly and leave political theatrics to Greece's past.
"We say no to chicken fights, false promises, meaningless rallies and plactic flags. We are against negative propaganda and blows below the belt," he said after calling elections a year early.
Although part of his plan is to make Greece less of a wild and unpredictable Balkan country and more of a steadily progressing, modern EU state, that placid approach left many voters cold.
Simitis proved himself a solid tactician by replacing late socialist party founder Andreas Papandreou as premier after he resigned in poor health in January.
He went on to win the party leadership and clearly thought an election win would cement his control of party and country but his lack of experience in a national campaign is evident.
Evert's style is the opposite. A powerfully built man who is always in motion, he was nicknamed "the Bulldozer" for his "Just Do It" approach to demolishing problems as Athens' mayor.
While Simitis sat back and waited for victory, Evert plunged into an intense national campaign, criss-crossing the country and barnstorming through mountain villages and distant islands.

"I'm spontaneous, and being spontaneous is not good politics these days. But I won't sit back and simply read off numbers over my little glasses," he said in a derisive dig at Simitis' granny glasses and professorial campaign style.
Simitis quickly changed his glasses.

Among the curious campaign twists has been the economic role reversal. Evert, a belt-tightening conservative, is offering a welter of costly promises while Simitis, once a free-spending socialist, is vowing tough fiscal policies to eliminate debt.
The blurring of ideological lines and lack of any personal charisma has left voters confused, undecided and turned off. Polls show more than 50 percent have little or no or interest in the outcome.

"What this 50 percent shows is that Greek elections are not as hot as they once were. The stakes are not as high," said MRB polling expert Christina Badouna. "The stakes are not clear to the electorate and people are more relaxed about how they vote."
That has been reflected in one of the quietest campaigns in 20 years, with few signs in the streets that an election is in the offing.
Some diplomats hoped this meant Greece's turbulent history since World War Two and its highly-polarized electorate since the fall of a military junta in 1974 were mellowing.

Many also applauded the absence of political giants such as conservative leader Constantine Karamanlis, who reestablished democracy, or Papandreou, who guided the Greek left back into mainstream politics.
"At last we're dealing with normal men again. People who feel they just represent a policy instead of personifying a nation and 3,000 years of history," said another EU diplomat.
That "normality" means Simitis and Evert are "just men" in their parties' eyes, too, and whoever loses on Sunday may lose his job quickly as party leader. --Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
